questions.prompt: An incremental gradient pass on \(f = f_1 + \cdots + f_m\)
questions.explanation: The pass updates the parameter after each block, so later blocks see the new point. Summing every gradient at the original point is the batch step. Reusing one block's gradient for the others ignores the data in those blocks. Setting gradients to zero is the stationarity condition for a minimizer, not the pass.

questions.prompt: Let \(f_1(u) = \tfrac12(u - 2)^2\) and \(f_2(u) = \tfrac12(u - 6)^2\). Start at \(u = 0\) and take step length \(1\), with \(f_1\) first. Where does one incremental pass end?
questions.explanation: The block gradients are \(u - 2\) and \(u - 6\). The first update is \(0 - (0 - 2) = 2\). The second, at the new point, is \(2 - (2 - 6) = 6\). The minimizer of the sum is \(4\), so the pass did not stop at a stationary point of \(f_1 + f_2\). Reporting \(2\) stops after the first block. Reporting \(4\) is the minimizer of the sum. Reporting \(8\) is the batch step of length \(1\) from \(0\), which uses both gradients at the original point.

questions.prompt: After the pass of length \(1\) that ends at \(6\), the next pass through the same two quadratics
questions.explanation: From \(6\) the first block sends the point to \(6 - (6 - 2) = 2\), and the second sends it back to \(2 - (2 - 6) = 6\). The full gradient at \(6\) is \(4\), not zero. The minimizer of the sum is \(4\), which this constant step never uses as an endpoint. A batch step of length \(1\) from \(0\) ends at \(8\), a different point. Step length \(1\) is a legal step; the second derivative of each block is \(1\), so this step lands on that block's minimizer.

questions.prompt: Put one incremental pass in order. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The pass needs a starting parameter before any block can be evaluated. The first step produces the point at which the next gradient is computed. Later blocks repeat that pattern. The comparison with a batch step is available only after the pass has a final point. Summing every gradient first would be the batch method.

steps: Start the pass at the current parameter.
Subtract the step length times the first block's gradient, evaluated at that point.
Evaluate the next block's gradient at the updated point, and step again.
After the last block, keep the updated parameter. It is not the sum of every block gradient at the original point.

questions.prompt: For \(f_1(u) = \tfrac12(u - 2)^2\) and \(f_2(u) = \tfrac12(u - 6)^2\), which statements about step lengths hold?
questions.explanation:
From \(6\), step length \(1\) returns to \(6\), and the full gradient \(2\cdot 6 - 8 = 4\) is not zero.
• A pass of length \(t\) sends \(u\) to \((1 - t)^2 u + t(1 - t)\cdot 2 + t\cdot 6\). The fixed point of that map is \(2(4 - t)/(2 - t)\). At \(t = 1\) it equals \(6\). As \(t\) tends to \(0\) it tends to \(4\).
• A constant step can sit away from a stationary point. Letting the length tend to zero removes that bias, and an infinite sum of lengths is what still lets the iterates travel. That pair is the usual requirement.
• Step length \(1\) ends at \(6\), not at \(4\). The batch step of length \(1\) from \(0\) ends at \(8\), not at the incremental endpoint \(6\).
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.
options: Step length \(1\) makes every later pass end at \(6\), where the full gradient equals \(4\), not zero.
The repeated-pass endpoint for a constant step \(t \in (0, 2)\) is \(2(4 - t)/(2 - t)\), which tends to the minimizer \(4\) as \(t\) tends to \(0\).
Steps that tend to \(0\) and whose lengths sum to infinity are the usual requirement for a stationary limit.
A larger constant step always reaches the minimizer \(4\) in one pass.
An incremental pass of any positive length matches the batch step of that same length.

questions.prompt: A block gradient equals \(a u + b\). After a step of length \(t\) from the scalar \(u\), the updated value equals
questions.explanation: One block step subtracts \(t\) times the gradient, so the new value is \(u - t(au + b)\). Every name appears: the point, the step length, and the two coefficients of the gradient. Dropping \(t\) subtracts the whole gradient. Using \(u + t(au + b)\) climbs the block. Freezing \(u\) inside the gradient and also adding \(t u\) double-counts the point.

questions.prompt: A note runs the pass of length \(1\) on \(f_1(u) = \tfrac12(u - 2)^2\) and \(f_2(u) = \tfrac12(u - 6)^2\), starting at \(0\), with \(f_1\) first. Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The first gradient \(0 - 2 = -2\) and the first update \(2\) are correct. The second block of an incremental pass is evaluated at \(2\), where the gradient is \(2 - 6 = -4\), and the update is \(6\). Evaluating the second gradient at the original point is the batch construction. That false step is what makes a finite pass differ from a summed gradient.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two arrows from the origin</title><line x1="46" y1="161.7" x2="250" y2="161.7"/><polygon points="250,161.7 243.6,164.4 243.6,159" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="138.7" y1="176" x2="138.7" y2="28"/><polygon points="138.7,28 141.5,34.4 136,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="248" y="175.7" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="144.7" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="138.7" y1="161.7" x2="235.9" y2="118.3"/><polygon points="235.9,118.3 231.2,123.4 228.9,118.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="243.9" y="110.3" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">g</text><line x1="138.7" y1="161.7" x2="60.1" y2="42.3"/><polygon points="60.1,42.3 65.9,46.2 61.3,49.2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="52.1" y="34.3" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">d</text></svg>
steps: The first block gradient at \(0\) is \(-2\).
The second block gradient is evaluated at the original point \(0\), so it equals \(-6\).
Evaluated at the updated point \(2\), the second gradient is \(-4\), and the second update is \(2 - (-4) = 6\).
reasons: The second block is evaluated at the updated point, not at the start of the pass.
The first gradient at \(0\) is not \(-2\).
The second gradient at the updated point \(2\) is not \(-4\).

questions.prompt: On the same two quadratics, start at \(u = 0\) with step length \(1/2\), and take \(f_1\) first. Where does one incremental pass end?
questions.explanation: The first update is \(0 - \tfrac12(0 - 2) = 1\). The second is \(1 - \tfrac12(1 - 6) = 1 + 2.5 = 3.5\). The batch step of this same length ends at \(4\), the minimizer. Reporting \(1\) stops after the first block. Reporting \(4\) is that batch result. Reporting \(6\) is the pass of length \(1\).

questions.prompt: A constant step and a step that tends to zero differ because
questions.explanation: On the two quadratics, step length \(1\) settles at the pass endpoint \(6\), where the full gradient is \(4\). The fixed endpoint \(2(4 - t)/(2 - t)\) tends to \(4\) only as \(t\) tends to \(0\). A vanishing step is not a batch step of fixed length. A constant step of length \(1\) does not finish at the minimizer. Swapping the two blocks at a finite step changes the intermediate point, so the order matters.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.
options: a constant step can settle away from a stationary point, while a vanishing step removes that bias
a vanishing step is the same update as a batch gradient of fixed length
a constant step always finishes a smooth sum in one pass
the order of the blocks never changes a finite step

questions.prompt: Recursive least squares, unlike an incremental pass that minimizes each block alone, minimizes
questions.explanation: The recursive step keeps every earlier block as a quadratic and appends the new linear residual. One Gauss-Newton step finishes that stacked cost. Minimizing only the newest block is a different pass: on \(\tfrac12(u-2)^2\) and \(\tfrac12(u-6)^2\), length \(1\) ends at \(6\), while the joint minimizer is \(4\). A constant-length gradient step is the incremental method itself. A spectral decomposition reads singular values.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a column of two labels</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">p</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">q</text></svg>
options: only the newest block, forgetting every earlier block
the full gradient with a constant step and no least-squares solve
a spectral decomposition of the data matrix
the old quadratic plus the new linear block, in one Gauss-Newton step

questions.prompt: On \(f_1(u) = \tfrac12(u - 2)^2\) and \(f_2(u) = \tfrac12(u - 6)^2\), the batch step of length \(1/2\) from \(u = 0\) uses the full gradient. Where does it land?
questions.explanation: The full gradient is \(2u - 8\), so at \(0\) it equals \(-8\). The second derivative of the sum is \(2\), and length \(1/2\) is the exact Newton step: \(0 - \tfrac12(-8) = 4\). That point is the minimizer. The incremental pass of the same length ends at \(3.5\), not here. Reporting \(-8\) is the gradient. Reporting \(8\) is the batch step of length \(1\).

questions.prompt: If a block residual is nonlinear, the incremental Gauss-Newton step has to rebuild the Jacobian at the updated estimate. Rebuilding it on every new block is what turns recursive least squares into
questions.explanation: A nonlinear measurement has a Jacobian that depends on the estimate. The next block is linearized at the latest estimate, which is the extended update. Keeping the first Jacobian forever is a frozen linear model. A simplex basis change is a pivot in a linear program. Ignoring the new block does not use the measurement that the update exists to include.
